today.name: Filament by Galaxy
today.tagline: Move data using your terminal or agent. Fast & open source.
today.description: Filament is a data replication engine written in Go. It supports full loads, incremental replication, and change data capture (CDC). You can run Filament as a standalone binary or embed it in a Go application.

yesterday.name: Omnigraph
yesterday.tagline: Open source graph database for your AI agents
yesterday.description: Omnigraph is an open-source object-storage native graph database with branching and typed ontology. It allows AI agents safely collaborate on shared knowledge. Give agents one typed graph with Git-like branching, review, and merge for every write, so changes can be validated before becoming shared context. Run it on your own S3-compatible storage, with semantic, keyword, and hybrid search plus graph traversal in one query. No hosted memory API or proprietary storage required.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt 👋 Omnigraph is an open source graph database where agents can safely collaborate and write to the same graph.It has a typed ontology, branches and time travel, and hybrid search with graph traversal in the same query. Your graph lives in your own object storage in an open format.⭐ GitHub (MIT): github.com/ModernRelay/omnigraphWhat can you use it forMore and more work inside a company is done by agents. They read the same data, write to it, make decisions on it, act on it. Without one shared world model they can trust, every agent ends up with its own version of the truth.Omnigraph is a foundation for that shared world model. comments.text: Hey Product Hunt 👋I'm Richard, co-founder of HarnessRouter. Today we're launching Harness Memory, which gives agents built on HarnessRouter a long-term memory.Here's why we built it. Every agent we built kept forgetting things, like what a user told it yesterday or what it figured out last session. It was worse whenever we switched harnesses, say from Claude Code to Hermes, or from Pi to Codex, because we had to wire memory up all over again each time. We kept thinking memory should be part of the agent instead of something you glue on afterwards.So that's what Harness Memory does:It's built in. When you build an agent, HarnessRouter picks a memory engine that fits the agent's job and tells you why. The options are Mem0, Graphiti, Hindsight and ReMe, or you can bring your own. Some agents shouldn't remember anything, like a translator that only transforms input, and those get no memory at all.It works in every session. The agent recalls memory when each turn starts, uses it through tools during the turn, and records what it learned when the turn ends. You don't write any glue code.It works across harnesses. A Claude Code agent, a Hermes agent, and a Codex agent can share one memory. In our demo, Codex saves a weekend plan, and Claude Code recalls that plan in a completely new session.We built it for agents that serve lots of people, so we were strict about a few things:Every user of the agent gets their own piece of memory, kept apart from everyone else's. Each memory needs its own access grant. Without a grant there's no access, and a model can't widen its own access.Agents can forget, but only people can erase. We never give an agent erase memory via a tool. When a fact changes, Harness Memory saves a new version, so the history stays.Memory informs the agent, but never instructs it. Recalled memory reaches the agent fenced off from its instructions, and each record is labeled with who wrote it. On the Memory page, people can see, edit or delete what's stored.We also made it open. The memory layer is an open spec, the Harness Memory Protocol, which is the Memories chapter of the Unified Harness Protocol. Any memory service can plug in as a provider. If a provider doesn't support something, we report the gap rather than skip it silently.Harness Memory is available today in the open-source Community Edition, and on HarnessRouter Cloud.We'd love to hear from you:What's the one thing you most wish your agent remembered?Which memory engine should we support next?We're around all day, so ask us anything 🙌

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

No learning curve. Really cool concept, congrats on the launch!The idea of making agent-native computing accessible without the terminal/self-hosting overhead resonates a lot. I've been building in the OpenClaw space since day one, and the security threat vectors are...let's just say...terrible (putting it nicely lol). When you're giving an agent full shell access to your actual system, the attack vectors get pretty real pretty fast. Prompt injection, unintended file modifications, credential exposure, etc.Love that you guys are leaning into built-in sandboxing and running directly in the browser as the approach here. My current multi-agent OS includes a mixture of protocols, not just openclaw, so always looking for new tools and methods.

Full disclosure — I'm a big fan of Anthropic and actually built an app that works exclusively with Claude Desktop for secure local file search. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
